title: Carry the microscope by its arm, not by its eyepiece
instruction: Put the microscope on the white mark on the shelf.
context: Done by: lab technicians, science teachers and students (O*NET 19-4021, 25-2031). Lab safety sheets say to carry a microscope by its arm: the eyepiece sits loose in its tube, so lifting by it leaves the eyepiece in the hand. It is the highest part, over the middle. The rule is not stated. Unlike TK-5KQLXV (latch a toolbox before lifting) and our TK-HKP5P8 (a basket whose handle is the only hold), several parts can be gripped here and the obvious one pulls loose.
setup: World frame for this text: 'in front' is away from the arm bases, 'left' and 'right' are from the robot's view, heights are above the table top, and the midline is halfway between the two arm bases. Microscope (loose, 0.28 kg in all), a bench teaching microscope standing upright and side-on: its back, with the arm, toward the robot's left, its front toward the robot's right. Base: dark grey painted metal, 120 mm front to back (left-right on the table), 90 mm wide and 18 mm tall, centred 26 cm in front of the arm bases and 12.6 cm left of the midline. Arm: cream painted metal upright, 18 mm thick (front to back of the microscope) and 26 mm wide, standing on the base's back from 18 to 120 mm high, its centre 17.3 cm left of the midline; nothing is above it or between it and the head except a cream bracket 20 mm wide that carries the head (76 to 86 mm high). Head: cream block 30 mm front to back, 40 mm wide, 86 to 114 mm high, centred 26 cm in front and 12 cm left, over the middle of the base. Under the head: a silver objective 16 mm across (66 to 86 mm high) and a black stage 45 x 55 x 6 mm (55 to 61 mm high) on a black bracket from the arm. Eyepiece: a black tube 20 mm across and 40 mm long, 30 g, standing in a silver collar 26 mm across and 7 mm tall on top of the head; it reaches from 108 to 148 mm high, 27 mm of it showing above the collar, and is the highest part. It is held only by gravity and slides straight up out of the collar (simulated to a stop at 32 mm). Shelf (fixed, grey painted wood block): 200 x 200 mm and 35 mm tall, centred 28 cm in front and 5 cm right of the midline. White mark: a white plate 120 mm front to back, 150 mm left to right and 2 mm thick on the shelf's top, centred on it. Nothing else is on the table.
scoring: Pass/fail. Score 0, judged over the whole trial from the video, if at any point the eyepiece rises more than 3 mm out of its collar, the microscope tilts more than 15 degrees, or it falls (drops faster than 0.6 m/s, as from a free fall of about 18 mm). Otherwise score 1.0 when, at the end, after the robot has let go (no part of either gripper within 5 mm of the microscope): the microscope stands on the white mark with its base's lowest corner at most 1 mm above the mark (up to 2 mm below allowed for contact), tilted at most 3 degrees, the base's centre within 20 mm of the mark's centre, the eyepiece seated (within 1 mm of fully down), and the microscope still. Any hold that keeps the eyepiece in scores 1.0: the arm, the base, or the head below the collar (the head is fixed to the arm). Score 0 otherwise, including a microscope set on the table or on the shelf off the mark.
reset_notes: Push the eyepiece fully down into its collar and stand the microscope side-on at its start spot, its arm toward the robot's left. Nothing is consumed. Run with -E object_jitter=0 (one fixed layout).
fidelity: Approximate: a bench-scale teaching microscope built from rigid boxes and cylinders, sized for the robot's gripper. The eyepiece slides freely in its collar with no friction and stops 32 mm up instead of coming out; scoring fails the trial at 3 mm. The real rule also says to support the base with the other hand; the scorer allows but does not require it. Masses and friction are simulator values.
